title: Individual Differences
summary: Individual differences are the extent and kind of variations or similarities among people on psychological aspects such as intelligence, personality, interest and aptitude. In a large sample most people fall in the middle range and few in the extremes (e.g. height). Differences are consistent and form a stable pattern, unique to each person, and arise from the interaction of genetic and environmental factors: we inherit characteristics through genetic codes, but the phenotype (expressed form) depends on the socio-cultural environment (upbringing, house atmosphere, education, peers, teachers, media); examples: Dr B.R. Ambedkar and Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

Psychological assessment is the use of specific procedures to evaluate personal qualities, behaviours and abilities and to describe how people differ from or resemble others. A psychological test is a structured technique used to generate a carefully selected sample of behaviour. A good test is reliable (measures consistently – similar scores on separate occasions), valid (assesses what it intends to assess) and standardised (same procedure and conditions of administration, group norms so that a score can be compared, as a test score is only relative). Achievement tests measure what has been learnt; tests of ability (intelligence and aptitude) measure capacity as potential; personality tests measure characteristic ways of thinking, feeling and behaving.

Intelligence is the 'multifaceted abilities of people' and is functional. Binet and Simon (1905): 'ability to judge well, to understand well and to reason well'. Wechsler (1939): 'the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with the environment'. Gardner: 'the ability or skill to solve problems or to fashion products valued in cultural settings'; eight multiple intelligences – linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic. Galton made the first attempt to measure intelligence; Alfred Binet (France) gave the concept of mental age (MA) in 1905; William Stern (Germany) devised the intelligence quotient in 1912: IQ = (MA / CA) x 100 (mental age 12, chronological age 8: IQ = 12/8 x 100 = 150). Binet's test was revised as the Stanford–Binet test (1916); Wechsler scales: WAIS for adults and WISC for children aged 6–16. Intelligence tests are individual or group; on the basis of items they are verbal (need literacy), non-verbal (pictures or illustrations) and performance tests (concrete tasks); non-verbal and performance tests suit literate and illiterate people.

Aptitude is a combination of characteristics indicating an individual's capacity to acquire specific knowledge or skill after training (e.g. musical sensitivity). Intelligence relates to the ability to do certain things at a given time; aptitude is potential ability to perform a task; achievement is performance in a subject already learnt. Aptitude tests predict success in vocations (clerical, mechanical, musical, typing); multiple aptitude batteries: Differential Aptitude Test (DAT), General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB), Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB). Interest is measured by vocational interest tests and general interest inventories – paper-pencil tests matching a person's interest with success in occupations.

Personality is a person's unique and relatively stable behaviour pattern, consistent across situations and over time. Allport (1937): 'the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustment to his environment'. Perspectives: trait (traits grouped into types such as introversion–extraversion), psychodynamic (Freud: unconscious needs and conflicts), socio-cultural (personality acquired through interaction and social norms) and humanistic (freedom and growth, optimistic). Measures: (A) objective or self-report measures – a questionnaire or inventory with closed or open statements: NEO-PI-R (Costa and McCrae, Five-Factor Model: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness), 16 PF (Cattell, for ages 16 and above, 16 primary traits and five global factors), Indian inventories (Bell Adjustment, Maslow Security–Insecurity, Maudsley in Hindi, Jodhpur Multiphasic); (B) projective or indirect measures – unstructured, ambiguous stimuli on which the person projects latent or unconscious feelings, needs, emotions and motives: Rorschach Ink Blot Test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank; (C) situational measures – behaviour is observed in purposefully designed situations, effective for leadership, dominance, responsibility, extraversion–introversion: the Character Education Enquiry (Hartshorne and May: altruism, honesty, self-control), OSS tests in World War II, Situational Stress Test.

Differentiate between intelligence, aptitude and achievement (two points).

Intelligence is the ability to do certain things at a given time; aptitude is the potential ability to learn a particular skill after training; achievement is performance in a subject with which the person is familiar.
What is standardisation of a test?
Establishing the same procedure and conditions of administration and group norms so that scores are uniform, objective and interpretable relative to others.

sa: Explain the properties of a good psychological test.

A good test is reliable (it gives consistent scores on different occasions), valid (it measures what it claims to measure and predicts relevant behaviour) and standardised (uniform procedure and group norms so scores can be compared).
Describe the types of intelligence tests.

Individual tests are given to one person at a time and group tests to many; by items, verbal tests need understanding of words (literate only), non-verbal tests use pictures and performance tests use concrete tasks; the last two suit literate and illiterate people.
Explain the nature of individual differences and their causes.

Most people fall in the middle range of any trait; differences are consistent and stable and unique to each person; they arise from the interaction of heredity (genetic codes) and the environment (upbringing, education, peers, media), as with Ambedkar and Kalam.

The person reports on himself in a questionnaire or inventory with closed- or open-ended statements; examples are NEO-PI-R (five factors) and 16 PF (16 primary traits) and Indian inventories such as the Bell Adjustment Inventory.

Behaviour is observed in purposefully designed situations; they assess leadership, dominance, responsibility and honesty; examples are the Character Education Enquiry tests (Hartshorne and May), the OSS selection tests and the Situational Stress Test.
Explain the perspectives of personality (any three).

Trait perspective describes personality by traits and types; psychodynamic stresses unconscious needs and conflicts (Freud); socio-cultural stresses social and cultural norms learnt through interaction; humanistic stresses freedom and growth.
la: Discuss the nature and definition of intelligence and the tools to measure it.

Intelligence is the multifaceted, functional ability of people. Binet and Simon defined it as the ability to judge, understand and reason well; Wechsler as the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment; Gardner proposed eight multiple intelligences. Binet gave mental age (1905) and Stern IQ = MA/CA x 100 (1912); tests include Stanford–Binet and the Wechsler scales (WAIS, WISC); tests may be individual or group, verbal, non-verbal or performance.
Explain aptitude and interest and how they are assessed.

Aptitude is the capacity to acquire a specific skill after training; it differs from intelligence and achievement. Aptitude tests (clerical, mechanical, musical, typing) predict vocational success; batteries are DAT, GATB and ASVAB. Interest is measured by vocational interest tests (paper-pencil tests matching interest with occupations) and general interest inventories.
Discuss the techniques of personality assessment.

Personality is the stable, unique behaviour pattern (Allport). Self-report measures use inventories (NEO-PI-R, 16 PF); projective measures use ambiguous stimuli (Rorschach, TAT, Rotter's sentences) to reveal unconscious motives; situational measures observe behaviour in designed situations (Hartshorne–May, OSS, Situational Stress Test). Perspectives are trait, psychodynamic, socio-cultural and humanistic.
What is psychological assessment? Explain the need for it and the properties of a test.

Psychological assessment uses specific procedures to evaluate personal qualities, behaviours and abilities and to describe how people are similar or different; everyday judgments like 'nice' or 'genius' are error-prone, so scientific tests aim at minimum error. A test must be reliable, valid and standardised. Achievement, ability and personality tests are used.
